justification:
Fresh read of the whole article, independent of the round-1 review. It clears the bar for 'sql injection prevention c#': a genuine, self-contained exploit runs against an in-memory SQLite table (never a real system), and the piece then goes past every competitor I read in depth rather than breadth. Microsoft's own SQL Server injection page (fetched in full) explains the mechanism with a static, non-executable ShipCity/OrdersTable example and stays at the conceptual level; Snyk's EF Core post (fetched) compares FromSqlRaw/FromSqlInterpolated but has no least-privilege discussion and no executed output; Acunetix's post (fetched) mentions least privilege in one line but shows no working exploit and never touches the numeric-field escaping failure or FromSqlRaw/FromSqlInterpolated at all. This article is the only one of the four that: (1) shows escaping fail on a second, differently-shaped injection point (an unquoted numeric id) instead of asserting escaping is fragile, (2) runs FromSqlInterpolated against FromSqlRaw with the same attacker string and prints the actual leaked admin row, and (3) demonstrates least privilege's real limit -- a read-only SQLite connection blocks the DROP with a genuine SQLITE_READONLY (error 8) but still leaks every row via UNION SELECT. That closing move is original synthesis, not something any of the four sources says outright.

I independently re-verified all three round-1 reviews' findings against the current text rather than taking 'fixed' on trust: (a) round-1 adsense's only issue -- quoting Microsoft's Redmond/OrdersTable example almost verbatim -- is gone; the article now paraphrases the semicolon/comment mechanism in its own words ('Microsoft's own SQL injection guide names the identical shape... because "the semicolon (;) denotes the end of one query and the start of another"') and keeps its own account-table example throughout, no lifted example. (b) round-1 technical's major finding -- a false claim that CWE-89 'opens with' reading confidential data -- is corrected; I re-fetched CWE-89's live Common Consequences table myself and it confirms the article's current wording ('lists "Execute Unauthorized Code or Commands" first and "Read Application Data" second') is now accurate. (c) round-1 technical's two minor sourcing gaps (the batching/NextResult mechanism and the SQLite storage-class comparison rule) are now both cited inline to the Batching and Datatypes pages, which I fetched and confirmed word-for-word match the article's quotes ('executes up to the first [statement] that returns results', 'executes any remaining statements that haven't been consumed by NextResult()'). None of these was papered over -- each is a substantive rewrite of the specific sentence, not a hedge word bolted on.

Plagiarism/paraphrase check: I web-searched five distinctive original (non-quoted) sentences from the article ('the escaping helper was never wrong; it was only ever an answer to one character', 'a login bypass and a wiped table are the same bug at different depths') and found no matches anywhere -- this is the article's own phrasing, not paraphrased from a source. Every inline quotation I checked (OWASP's two escaping/parameters lines, Microsoft's SQL Server 'prematurely terminating' and comment-mark lines, the Batching page's ExecuteReader/NextResult/Dispose lines, and OWASP's least-privilege guidance) is verbatim against the live page and supports exactly the clause it's attached to.

Structure: headings are specific to the content on this page, not templated, and read nothing like the sibling articles I compared (transactions-and-acid, sql-joins, relational-model-and-keys all use question-form or noun-phrase headings but none share phrasing, opening style or exercise wording with this one) or with recursion.md/big-o-notation.md from other pillars. All three exercises sit mid-article at the point they're relevant, vary in form (predict-then-check on row order, extend-the-attack-then-check on the numeric endpoint, write-a-fix on the allow-listed sort column), and none exposes its output panel above the collapsed solution. No filler intro/outro, no restated title, no keyword stuffing, no invented experience or statistics, no formulaic triplets or empty signposting anywhere in the piece. node tools/check-article.mjs reports 0 errors/0 warnings (words=4566, within the 4,000-7,000 band); node tools/run-code.mjs passes all 22 blocks/11 executed. The one soft crosslink (to the planned exceptions article) is recorded in docs/crosslinks/databases/sql-injection-and-parameters.md and is a sensible, narrow tie-in (throw vs throw ex on the caught SqliteException), not a dead end.

Why not a 10: Microsoft's own page, while less concrete about .NET code, still covers more of the attack surface than this article's scope calls for (stored-procedure truncation attacks, LIKE-clause wildcard escaping, input-validation checklists) -- material this article's plan intentionally leaves out to stay focused on the parameters/EF Core/least-privilege arc. That is a legitimate scope choice per CONTENT_PLAN's outline, not a defect, but it keeps this just short of 'clearly better than the best existing result' on raw coverage even though it is deeper and more rigorously demonstrated on everything it does cover.
